tests.topic: A neighbourhood newsstand closes after forty years: the owner explains that few people still buy a paper on the way to work, and what he will miss is not the sales but the customers who stopped to talk. The kiosk will reopen as a parcel pick-up point.

A cousin who lives abroad cooks carbonara with cream and onion; the grandmother says nothing but makes it again the next day her way: eggs, cured pork cheek, pecorino and pepper, with the eggs added off the heat so they do not turn into an omelette.

In one family Christmas has a strict rule: Christmas Eve dinner with the mother's parents, who serve fish, and Christmas Day lunch with the father's, who serve meat, and the next year the other way round. The year the rule is broken for a trip, both grandmothers take offence.

A mother and her fourteen-year-old daughter shop for an outfit for a cousin's wedding. The mother wants an elegant dress and proper shoes, the daughter wants trousers and trainers; they settle on something neither had in mind when they left home.

The exam at the end of middle school, the first real exam in an Italian pupil's life: written papers and then an oral in front of all the teachers, where each pupil presents a subject of their own choice. One girl's preparation, her nerves in the corridor, and how it went.

A sixteen-year-old spends the summer helping at a beach club: he opens two hundred umbrellas at seven in the morning, rakes the sand and carries sunbeds. He discovers that other people's holiday is somebody's hard work, and what he does with his first pay.

Every resident of Italy has a family doctor who costs nothing at the visit: you sit in the waiting room, ask who is last, and wait your turn. A doctor who has known the same family for twenty years decides whether a prescription or a specialist is needed.

Since high-speed trains link Rome and Milan in about three hours, a father who used to fly for work takes the train. He compares the two journeys door to door (the trip to the airport, the checks, the waiting) and explains what he does with the time on board.

Friends organise their weekly five-a-side football match: one player has pulled out at the last minute, the pitch is booked for nine and must be paid whether they are ten or not. They decide whom to call, who brings the bibs, and how to split the cost.

In the Middle Ages the rich families of San Gimignano, a small Tuscan town, each built a tower beside their house, and each wanted the tallest. There were once about seventy; the town then ruled that none could rise above the town hall's, and fourteen still stand.

When a very high tide is expected in Venice sirens sound, raised wooden walkways are laid out and shopkeepers lift their goods off the floor. One shopkeeper's routine, and what changed for him once mobile barriers at the entrances to the lagoon could be raised.

The leader of the Giro d'Italia wears pink because the sports newspaper that founded the race is printed on pink paper. The race is usually decided on the high mountain passes, where fans camp for days and paint riders' names on the road; the passage explains why the climbs matter more than the flat stages.

The Pinocchio of the book is not the one of the cartoon: Collodi published the story in parts in a children's paper and first ended it with the puppet hanged from an oak. Readers protested, the paper asked for more, and only then did the Fairy save him.

Two travellers on a delayed train realise that they will miss their connection at Bologna by five minutes. They ask the conductor what to do: whether their tickets are valid on the next train, how long the wait is, and whether a slower regional train would get them there sooner.

In 1610 Galileo pointed his telescope at Jupiter and saw small stars beside it that changed position every night. He understood that they were moons going round the planet, which meant that not everything in the sky turned around the Earth.

Long before they were American, a strong blue cloth was made in Genoa for the trousers of sailors and port workers and sold across Europe under the city's name. How the same kind of cloth later reached the workers of California, and why Genoa still tells the story.

In the traditional Sicilian puppet theatre, wooden knights in metal armour almost a metre tall fight the battles of Charlemagne's knights. The story was told in episodes, one each evening for months, and the audience came back every night; a few families of puppeteers still perform it.

To see Leonardo's Last Supper in Milan you book months ahead and enter in a small group for fifteen minutes. Leonardo painted on a dry wall with a method of his own so that he could work slowly, and the paint began to come away within his lifetime.

Two pupils in the last year of middle school talk about which upper school to choose: one feels pushed towards the scientific liceo by her parents but likes the technical institute she saw at the open day; the other has not decided at all.

Digging at Pompeii, archaeologists kept finding empty spaces in the hardened ash. In the nineteenth century one of them had liquid plaster poured into a hole before digging further: when it set, it had the shape of a person who died in the eruption of 79 AD, down to the folds of the clothes.

The oranges grown on the plain below Etna are red inside. The colour comes from the difference between warm days and cold winter nights near the volcano: the same trees planted where nights are mild give ordinary orange fruit. They are picked from December to spring.

For centuries shepherds walked their flocks every autumn from the mountains of Abruzzo to the warm plains of Puglia along wide grass tracks, and back in spring. Most sheep now travel by lorry, but a few families still make the journey on foot, and walkers join them.

A family keeps the cardboard suitcase with which a great-grandfather sailed to America in the early 1900s. He meant to stay three years, sent money home every month for a house, and came back after twelve; his letters show what he missed and what he did not.

Two friends at the January sales: one wants a jacket at half price that she does not need, the other points out that she already has two like it. They agree on a rule for the afternoon: buy only what was on the list written at home.

The Vespa was designed just after the war by an engineer of aircraft who disliked motorcycles: he covered the engine so that it would not dirty clothes, added a shield for the legs and made the wheel easy to change. Its name came from its wasp-like shape and sound.

The cheapest seats at La Scala are in the gallery under the roof, and they hold the most demanding audience: opera lovers who know every note and boo a singer who gets one wrong. A student queues for hours for a ticket and watches her neighbours as much as the stage.

At twenty Guglielmo Marconi experimented in the attic of the family house near Bologna. To learn whether his signal had crossed the hill behind the garden he sent his brother to the far side with a receiver and a rifle: one shot in the air meant it had arrived.

In Gianni Rodari's 'Favole al telefono' a travelling salesman phones his daughter every evening at nine to tell her a story. The stories are very short because long-distance calls were expensive, and that limit is exactly what makes each of them work.

In the 1970s only about a hundred wolves were left in Italy, in the central mountains; protected by law, they have spread back along the Apennines and into the Alps. Walkers are pleased, shepherds are not, and many now rely on large white guard dogs and electric fences.

Bologna has tens of kilometres of porticoes: in the Middle Ages houses were extended over the street on wooden posts to make room for the university's students, and the city then made the covered walk compulsory. Today you can cross the centre in the rain without an umbrella.

At two in the morning a father needs medicine for his daughter's fever. His usual pharmacy is closed, but the notice on its door names the one on night duty across town, where he rings a bell and is served through a small window.

Rowing a gondola looks easy and is a regulated trade: for a long time the licence passed from father to son, today there is a school, an exam on rowing with a single oar and on the canals, and a limited number of licences. One young man's year as a substitute.

An only child spends August in a house by the sea with five cousins: at first the noise, the queue for the bathroom and the shared room annoy him, but back in his quiet flat in September he finds he misses all of it.

An exchange student orders a cappuccino after lunch and the waiter smiles. Her Italian friend explains the habits (milk in the morning, an espresso after a meal, coffee drunk standing at the counter because it costs less) and admits that nobody will actually stop her.

Two pizzas, two ideas: the Neapolitan one rises for many hours, cooks in about ninety seconds in a very hot wood oven and has a soft, high edge; the Roman one is rolled thin and comes out crisp. Why people from each city defend their own.

A visitor from abroad is surprised by the 'coperto' on a restaurant bill: a small fixed charge per person for bread and table service. The passage explains what it covers, why a tip is welcome but not expected, and why some restaurants have dropped it.

The oral test at the teacher's desk, a habit of Italian schools: the teacher runs a finger down the register and the class holds its breath. A boy who has studied offers to go as a volunteer so that his friend, who has not, is safe for another day.

The Mediterranean diet is not pizza and pasta every day: as doctors described it in villages of southern Italy, it meant mostly vegetables, beans, bread and olive oil, a little fish and meat only on feast days. Why the people who ate that way out of poverty lived so long.

A boy tells his best friend that his family is moving from Bari to Turin because of his father's job. He is worried about the new school and the cold; the friend finds reasons it might not be so bad and they plan how to stay in touch.

At fourteen an Italian can ride a small scooter after passing a test. A boy wants one for his birthday; his parents set conditions: the course first, a helmet always fastened, no passengers, and half of the insurance paid from his own savings.

The Palio of Siena is a horse race around the main square that lasts about ninety seconds: seventeen districts, of which only ten run each time, riders without saddles, and a horse that can win even if its rider has fallen. The rivalry between districts lasts all year.

Galvani thought that a dead frog's leg moved because of electricity inside the animal; Volta believed it came from the two metals touching it. To prove it he stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by wet card and built the first battery, and the volt is named after him.

Milan fashion week seen by someone who lives there: blocked streets, people photographed on the pavement for what they wear, black cars double-parked. Behind a show of fifteen minutes are months of work by tailors and technicians whom nobody photographs.

A pupil from a technical school starts two weeks of work experience in a car repair shop. The owner tells him what he may touch and what he may not, why he will sweep the floor on the first day, and what he will be allowed to do by the end if he watches carefully.

The floats of the carnival of Viareggio are moving figures of papier-mache as tall as a building, each worked from inside by dozens of people pulling ropes and levers. They are built over many months in large sheds by family workshops, shown on a few Sundays, and then taken apart.

The churches of Ravenna are plain brick outside and covered inside with mosaics fifteen centuries old. The tiny pieces of glass were set at slightly different angles on purpose, so that the gold seems to move as the light changes or as the visitor walks.

Until 1861 the peninsula was divided into several states with their own rulers, coins and borders. The passage tells how Garibaldi sailed to Sicily with about a thousand volunteers in red shirts, and why almost every Italian town has a street or square named after him.

In spring the rice fields of the plain between Vercelli and Novara are flooded and look like one huge mirror. The water protects the young plants from cold nights; once thousands of women pulled out the weeds by hand, bent over for eight hours, where one machine passes now.

A boy visiting Venice asks a guide how stone palaces can stand on water. She explains that they rest on thousands of wooden posts driven into the mud, why the wood has not rotted after centuries without air, and what really damages the buildings today.

In the Middle Ages Amalfi, Pisa, Genoa and Venice were independent cities that grew rich on sea trade and often fought one another. Their four symbols are on the flag of the Italian navy today, and once a year crews from the four cities meet again in a rowing race.

A girl finds in the wardrobe a jacket her mother wore in the 1990s and wears it to school, where it is admired. Her mother cannot believe it is fashionable again; the two visit a second-hand shop together and disagree about what is 'old' and what is 'vintage'.

Italy has many earthquakes because it lies where two great plates of the Earth's crust push against each other, and the Apennines are the result. What pupils practise at school: under the desk while it shakes, then out in a line without running and never by the lift.

A pupil has to learn the opening lines of Dante's Inferno by heart and cannot get past the third. At dinner her grandfather, who left school at fourteen, recites them without a mistake; he explains how he was taught, and she tries his method.

On a hot July afternoon two friends walking home notice that the avenue with plane trees feels much cooler than the new square paved in stone. They talk about why, where they would plant trees in their neighbourhood, and who waters them in the first years.

A boy spends a whole season on the bench of his youth football team and thinks of giving up. The coach puts him on for the last twenty minutes of the final match; he does not score, but he understands why he kept coming to training.

Tourists complain about the brown heaps of dried sea plants on some Mediterranean beaches, and towns used to cart them away. Biologists explain that the plant grows only in clean water and that the heaps protect the sand from winter waves; some beaches now put up signs instead.

In an old Milanese 'casa di ringhiera' every flat opens onto a long shared balcony around a courtyard. Once these were workers' homes with one toilet per floor, where neighbours knew everything about each other; now the same flats are fashionable and expensive.

Many Italian historic centres are limited traffic zones where cameras photograph every number plate and only residents may enter. A tourist in a hired car follows the navigator into one and receives the fine months later; why cities chose this instead of gates or guards.

A grandmother who sewed dresses at her kitchen table for the neighbourhood and a granddaughter who writes software at the same table for a firm in another city: both work from home and both have customers in a hurry, but only one of them ever met her customers.

A three-day school trip to Florence: the rules read out on the coach, the long queue for the museum, the teacher who counts heads every ten minutes. What the pupils remember afterwards is not the paintings but the talk in the hotel room at night.

A family decides that during dinner all phones go in a basket by the door. The first to break the rule is the father, for a work message; after a month the children admit that dinner lasts longer and that they know more about each other's day.

A visitor finds Tuscan bread tasteless on the first day: it is made without salt. The usual explanations (an old tax on salt, and the very salty ham and cheese it is eaten with) and why by the end of the week he prefers it.

A girl gets ten euros of pocket money a week and wants headphones that cost a hundred and twenty: she counts the weeks, gives up the afternoon snack at the bar, and her parents promise to pay the second half if she saves the first.

Two members of a library reading group for teenagers argue after watching the film of the novel they have just read: one is angry that a character was cut, the other thinks the ending works better on screen. Each gives one concrete example.

A village grocery survives after a supermarket opens two kilometres away: it cannot win on price, so the owner delivers to elderly customers, sells cheese from a local farm, and lets people pay at the end of the month.

How to tell a good gelato shop before tasting: the ice cream is not piled in high bright mountains, the pistachio is a dull brownish green, the banana is greyish, and the best shops keep it in covered metal tubs. Why bright colour means something was added.

The older sister leaves to study in Bologna and her brother finally gets the bigger room he always wanted. He finds the house too quiet, keeps her posters on the wall, and waits for the Sunday evening video call more than he would admit.

With the electronic register parents see a mark on their phone the same morning it is given. A boy who gets a four in maths can no longer wait for the right moment, so he decides to tell his mother himself before she opens the app.

A city boy staying on a farm that takes guests talks to the farmer's daughter, who is his age. He is surprised that she gets up at half past five to help with the milking before school; she is surprised that he has never seen where cheese comes from.

A mountain guide in the Dolomites turns his group back two hundred metres below the summit because clouds are building. The clients are disappointed and one complains about the money; the guide explains that his job is to bring people home, not to the top.

To play in a team an Italian teenager needs a medical certificate every year, and for competitions the visit includes a test of the heart at rest and after effort. A boy is nervous about the wires on his chest; the doctor explains what she is looking for and why.

Ferrara is flat, its centre is closed to cars, and nearly everyone cycles: pensioners with shopping bags on the handlebars, lawyers in suits, children on the way to school. A newcomer learns the unwritten rules and that the commonest crime in town is bicycle theft.

Florence had a cathedral with a hole in the roof too wide for any wooden frame. Brunelleschi won the competition by proposing to build the dome without one: two shells, one inside the other, and bricks laid in a herringbone pattern so that each ring held itself up.

Two friends visit the Uffizi on a free Sunday after a long queue. One wants to see every room; the other proposes choosing five works and really looking at them. They compare lists, argue over Botticelli, and agree on a meeting point.

A girl walks up to an Alpine glacier with a photograph her grandfather took at the same age. Along the path signs with dates show where the ice ended in each decade; she reaches the place in his picture and the ice is still forty minutes further up.

Every September a group of classmates meets for the auction of their fantasy football league: each has the same pretend budget to buy real players, and points depend on what those players do on Sunday. One boy spends almost everything on a single striker and regrets it by October.

The weekly comic 'Topolino' is sold at Italian newsstands, and most of its Disney stories are written and drawn in Italy. A boy finds his father's collection in the cellar, hundreds of small issues, and father and son discover that they like the same character.

A shoemaker in a side street explains to a boy why a pair of good leather shoes can be resoled five times and last twenty years, while glued trainers go in the bin after one. He has fewer customers every year and no apprentice.

Three friends rehearse in a garage for their first concert at the end-of-year school party. The neighbour has complained about the noise, the drummer keeps speeding up, and they must choose between a song everyone knows and one they wrote themselves.

A girl attends an ordinary school in the morning and the conservatory in the afternoon: three hours of violin a day, homework on the bus, no free Saturdays. She says what she has given up, and what she feels when a difficult passage finally comes out right.

In Orgosolo, a village in the mountains of Sardinia, hundreds of paintings cover the walls of the houses. A teacher and his pupils began them in the 1970s; they show shepherds, protests and village life, and residents decide what may be painted on their own wall.

On the western slope of Etna pistachio trees grow straight out of old lava where nothing else will. The growers pick only every second year and remove the buds in the year between so that the trees can rest; the nuts are gathered by hand because no machine can cross the rock.

A truffle hunter goes out before dawn with his dog and tells nobody where. Dogs have replaced pigs, which found the truffles just as well but ate them; the training starts with a puppy and a piece of cheese, and one good morning can pay for a month.

A boy who falls asleep during the first lesson admits to a friend that he is on his phone until one every night. The friend, who had the same problem, suggests a one-week experiment: the phone charges in the kitchen and they compare how they feel on Friday.

The university of Bologna, founded in the eleventh century, is considered the oldest in Europe. At the beginning it was the students who organised it: they chose the teachers, paid them, and could fine a professor who arrived late or did not finish the programme.

The eight-sided aluminium coffee pot found in almost every Italian kitchen was invented in 1933. Water boils in the base and steam pushes it up through the ground coffee; its shape has hardly changed, and families argue about whether it should ever be washed with soap.

The pizzica of the Salento was once danced, the story goes, to cure women bitten by a spider in the fields: musicians played for hours, sometimes days, until the patient stopped. Today the same fast rhythm fills squares at summer festivals and nobody needs a cure.

A foreign student living with an Italian family notices that nobody leaves the house in a tracksuit, not even to buy bread, and that the grandmother irons everything, including tea towels. The family explains the idea of making a good impression; the student is half convinced.

A boy cracks his phone screen and, instead of asking for a new phone, orders the part and follows a video guide. He loses a tiny screw and needs two attempts; it costs a fifth of the shop price and he learns what is inside the object he uses all day.

One girl writes every evening in a paper diary with a lock; her friend posts what she writes online. They compare: the first writes things she would tell nobody, the second chooses her words more carefully because she knows somebody will read them.

Next to many Italian churches there is an 'oratorio', a youth centre with a football pitch and table football, open to anyone in the afternoon. A boy who has just moved to the neighbourhood goes there alone, is put in goal because nobody else wants to be, and leaves with a team.

Every summer fires burn the dry scrub of southern Italy and the islands. Heat and wind spread them, but almost all are started by people, through carelessness or on purpose; yellow planes skim the sea to fill their tanks and drop the water on the flames.

In Matera families lived for centuries in homes dug into the rock, often with their animals. In the 1950s the district was called a national shame and its people were moved to new housing; decades later the same caves became hotels and the town's main attraction.

Two classmates wake up to three hundred messages in the class group chat, mostly stickers, with the one useful message about tomorrow's test lost in the middle. They discuss leaving, muting, or proposing a second group for school matters only.

Genoa is built on steep hills behind the port, so public lifts and small cable railways are part of the city transport like buses, and one ticket covers them all. A girl's daily way to school: a lift inside the rock, then a walk along a street that looks down on roofs.

An Italian grandmother is sure that a draught on the neck or going out with wet hair makes you ill, and insists on a scarf. Her granddaughter has learnt at school that colds come from viruses, tells her so, and then puts the scarf on anyway.

In many small mountain villages the fire brigade is made up of volunteers with other jobs. A baker leaves his oven to a colleague when the siren sounds; the passage follows one night call and explains why he has done this for twenty years without pay.

A grandmother from the South phones her grandson to wish him well on his name day, the day of the saint he is named after, and he does not know what she is talking about. For her generation it mattered as much as a birthday; she explains why and sends him pastries.

A grandmother tells her granddaughter about the day in 1946 when her own mother voted for the first time, as Italian women had just won the right: the queue in her best dress, the fear of spoiling the ballot paper, and why she kept talking about that morning for the rest of her life.

Pupils complain about fish on Fridays in the school canteen. The cook explains that a dietician decides the menu, that it changes with the seasons, and that the dishes children refuse most are served again in a different form rather than removed.

Why a group of small mountain towns near Belluno makes glasses for half the world: one workshop a century ago, then workers who left to open their own, until each family firm did one part of the frame. What a district is, and what happens when the big firms move work abroad.

How a wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano is made and judged: milk from the morning and the evening before, at least twelve months on wooden shelves, and an expert who taps every wheel with a small hammer and listens. Why the wheels that sound wrong lose the name.

In the first year of upper school a class elects its two representatives. One candidate promises a longer break and a new drinks machine; the other says honestly what a representative can do: speak for the class at the meeting with the teachers. Who wins and why.

Most Italian middle schools finish at about two o'clock and pupils eat lunch at home; some offer 'full time' with canteen and afternoon lessons. Two cousins in the two systems compare their days: one has free afternoons but homework alone, the other gets home at five with nothing left to do.

About fifty brown bears of a kind found nowhere else live in the mountains of Abruzzo. In autumn one sometimes walks into a village at night for the fruit trees and the bins; residents are told not to feed or follow it, and the passage explains why a bear that loses its fear of people is in danger.

Jesi, a small town in the Marche, has produced a surprising number of Olympic fencing champions from a single club. A girl starts there at eight because 'everyone does'; the passage explains how one good teacher and champions training beside beginners made a tradition.

On the night of 10 August Italians lie on beaches and in fields to look for shooting stars and make a wish. The 'stars' are grains of dust left by a comet that burn as the Earth passes through them every year; why you see more after midnight and far from the city.

In Cremona, the town of Stradivari, more than a hundred workshops still make violins by hand. One maker explains her work: spruce from an Alpine valley for the front, maple for the back, about two hundred hours for each instrument, and varnish made to her own recipe.

When the plague travelled on merchant ships, Venice made vessels arriving from infected ports wait at anchor and sent crews and goods to an island in the lagoon for forty days before they could enter the city. What life on that island was like, and why other ports copied the idea.

A beekeeper moves his hives by lorry at night, when the bees are all inside, following the flowers: acacia in May, lime in June, chestnut in the hills in July. Each stop gives a honey with a different colour and taste, and a hive left in the wrong place gives almost none.
